analysis.one_liner: Writes the right to get and provide contraception into federal law and blocks state restrictions on it.
analysis.headline: Introduced with 25 Democratic cosponsors and none from the other party, the bill died in the Senate Judiciary Committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would write the right to obtain contraceptives — and the right of nurses, doctors, and pharmacists to provide them — into federal law. It would strike down state or local rules that single out contraception and make it harder to get, including over objections under the federal Religious Freedom Restoration Act. Patients, providers, and the Justice Department could sue to enforce it. It never got a vote: it sat in the Senate Judiciary Committee from the day it was introduced until the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who uses contraception, and the health care providers who supply it. People in states moving to restrict contraception, emergency contraception, or related care would benefit most, because the bill would override those state rules and give patients and providers a way to sue to stop them. The bill's findings emphasize that barriers fall hardest on low-income people, people of color, rural residents, and others who already face the toughest access problems.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People who use or provide contraception

how_it_helps.text: Creates a statutory right for any person to obtain contraceptives and to use them, and a matching right for health care providers to provide contraception and information about it.
Bars government measures that single out contraception and impede access, and overrides state and local laws that restrict sale, provision, or use of any contraceptive the FDA has approved.

Lets the Justice Department, patients, and providers sue states and officials to strike down violating rules, awards attorney's fees to winning plaintiffs, and strips states of legal immunity from those suits.
Applies notwithstanding the Religious Freedom Restoration Act, so federal religious-freedom claims could not be used to block access to contraception.

Was a direct response to the Dobbs decision: its findings cite Justice Thomas's concurrence urging the Court to reconsider the 1965 precedent that established the constitutional right to contraception.

analysis.who_pays: State governments that restrict contraception would lose that authority and face lawsuits from the Justice Department and private plaintiffs, and would owe attorney's fees when they lose. Governments could no longer cite the federal Religious Freedom Restoration Act to defend restrictions. No industry bears a direct cost; the bill explicitly leaves insurance coverage rules untouched.

drawbacks.text: The bill applies notwithstanding the Religious Freedom Restoration Act, meaning it overrides that federal religious-liberty statute. That is the strongest good-faith objection: Congress would be declaring that religious-freedom claims cannot block contraception access.

It preempts broad swaths of state authority: no state or locality may enforce any law that restricts FDA-approved contraceptives or makes them harder to obtain, and a defendant can escape liability only by proving by clear and convincing evidence that a rule significantly advances safety with no less restrictive alternative.
Governments that lose a suit must pay the plaintiff's litigation costs and attorney's fees, and states can be sued by the Justice Department, patients, and providers without immunity.
It does nothing about cost: the bill explicitly does not affect insurance coverage rules, so it protects the legal right to obtain contraception without requiring any health plan to pay for it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — locking contraception access into federal statute at a moment when a Supreme Court justice had called for reconsidering the underlying constitutional precedent — is broad and touches most American adults at some point in their lives. The costs are real but concentrated: states lose the power to restrict contraception, religious-freedom defenses under federal law are set aside, and losing governments pay legal fees. The biggest design gap is that the bill protects the right to obtain contraception but deliberately does nothing to require insurance to cover it, so affordability is left unaddressed.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced and never received a committee or floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on July 26, 2022, weeks after the Supreme Court's Dobbs decision, and its findings quote Justice Thomas's concurrence calling for the Court to reconsider the precedents protecting contraception.
The same day, it was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee.
Twenty-five Senate Democrats cosponsored it; not a single Republican did.
The action history ends there: no committee vote, no floor vote, nothing further before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: State governments that want to restrict contraception kept their authority, since no federal statute now protects access. Contraception's legal protection still rests on court precedent rather than law — the very situation the bill was written to change.

for.name: Sen. Edward Markey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Right to Contraception Act on July 26, 2022, with a group of Democratic colleagues.

against.name: 50 of 50 Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: Gave the bill no support: none of the 50 Republicans cosponsored, and the bill never reached the floor.

against.name: Sen. Chuck Schumer
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor; it sat in committee until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All 25 cosponsors were Senate Democrats and no Republican signed on; the bill never reached a vote, so opposition shows up as absence of support rather than a recorded no.

industries.note: The bill bars states from restricting sale or use of any FDA-approved contraceptive, protecting the market for drugs and devices like pills, IUDs, and emergency contraception. That protection runs in the same direction as patient access.
Providers gain a statutory right to provide contraception and information about it, plus the power to sue on their own behalf and their patients' behalf, with attorney's fees available if they win.

The bill explicitly leaves insurance coverage rules alone, so insurers neither gain new obligations nor lose the discretion they have today. The right to obtain contraception would not come with any requirement that a plan pay for it.
